The post Genetic Analysis All But Confirms the Most Unique of Humpback Populations Is Actually a Subspecies appeared first on Good News Network.

Actual Article Body:
This breathtaking photograph is of an Arabian Sea humpback whale—the subject of a new genetic analysis that seems to confirm beyond a shadow of a doubt that it’s a totally different subspecies compared to its cousins in the Pacific or Atlantic.

Existing with a remarkably unique ecology, it’s been clear to anyone with experience that Arabian Sea humpbacks are just different, but until recently it was uncertain whether this was a recent or prehistoric development.

Published in Frontiers in Marine Science, a study leveraging more than 25 years of whale research in Oman supports the recognition of a 4th subspecies of humpback.

Led by the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) in close collaboration with Omani environmental authorities and other key local and international partners, the study compared genetic samples from Arabian Sea humpback whales with populations from across the world’s oceans, including mitochondrial DNA from 2,285 animals.

Results revealed high levels of genetic differentiation between the Arabian Sea population and the 3 currently-recognized humpback whale subspecies of the North Atlantic, North Pacific, and Southern Hemisphere, indicating very limited gene flow between them.

The Arabian Sea population also showed the lowest genetic diversity among the ocean regions examined. The findings support the potential recognition of the Arabian Sea population as Megaptera novaeangliae indica, named for the type species in Iraq.

“Arabian Sea humpback whales have long been an enigma to the scientific community. Their ecology is unlike that of any other known humpback whale population, and this new genetic work represents an important milestone in understanding how that uniqueness developed,” said the study’s lead author Dr. Rita Amaral with the WCS.

“The results clearly indicate the Arabian humpback whales have followed their own evolutionary trajectory for tens of thousands of years and support their recognition as a distinct subspecies.”

Arabian humpbacks are the only group in their race which neither migrate to breed nor feed. They remain in the seas off Oman all year round, and are even genetically distinct from whales as close by as the Indian Ocean. What explains this strange, sedentary lifestyle?

The authors, citing research conducted over the decades, detail that seasonal upwelling of deep oceanic nutrients, driven by the southwest monsoon, creates hyper-productive conditions more typical of those found in temperate climates where whales would typically migrate to feed.

Other humpbacks who’ve thusly migrated to cooler waters then return to the tropics to breed, but that unique upwelling allows the Arabian sea humpbacks to feed at tropical latitudes normally associated with breeding activities.

A study published for the International Whaling Commission in 2018 reviewed Arabian Sea humpback whale singing and found that it too is unique among the species. All males within a population share the same song patterns, which also tend to change progressively over time. Populations that do not overlap or exchange individuals have distinctly different songs, the study wrote, whereas populations in contact share some, or all patterns.

This provides more evidence for a theory on a separate Arabian subspecies, because while overlapping populations of Arabian humpbacks share song patterns, the IWC study found zero overlap between Arabian humpback and Indian Ocean humpback singing, strongly indicating populational isolation.

Now, this new study presents genetic analyses that shows the Arabian Sea whale lineages diverged between 43,000 and 113,000 years ago, depending on the group.
